Query-adaptive Recurrent Tokenization

Bavesh Balaji    Pranav Gopinath    Pouya Sadeghi    Sirisha Rambhatla ††thanks: Affiliation: Critical ML Lab Affiliation: University of Waterloo Affiliation: {bbalaji, p3gopina, pouya.sadeghi, sirisha.rambhatla}@@uwaterloo.ca
Abstract

Visual information worth extracting from an image and the token budget it warrants depend on the text query. Yet modern vision and vision-language models largely encode images independently of the query and allocate a fixed visual token budget to every input. We introduce the Query-Adaptive Recurrent Tokenizer (QART), a backbone-agnostic module that makes visual representations both query-steerable and budget-adaptive. QART steers the visual representation toward query-relevant evidence while adapting its token budget to the amount of information required. Its key principle is simple. Additional tokens are allocated until the visual features relevant to the query are represented with sufficient fidelity. Starting from frozen encoder features, QART recurrently constructs a compact representation and uses reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support to control token allocation. On Visual7W and VQAv2 , QART achieves 81.96% and 76.37% accuracy using only about 29 visual tokens, reducing token counts by 20–25×\times relative to dense VLM inputs. It further reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%. Together, these results show that visual representations need not be fixed in either content or capacity and can instead adapt to what each query requires.

1 Introduction

“A wealth of information creates a poverty of attention and a need to allocate that attention efficiently among the overabundance of information sources that might consume it.”

— Herbert A. Simon (1971)

An image contains evidence for many possible questions, and the visual information that matters depends on what is being asked Anderson et al. (2018); Hudson and Manning (2019); Pantazopoulos and Özyiğit (2025). In the same street scene, identifying the color of a traffic light requires evidence from a small region, whereas counting vehicles turning left requires information distributed across objects and their spatial relationships (Acharya et al., 2018; Rajabi and Košecká, 2024; Ishihara et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026; Sadeghi et al., 2026). Yet SOTA vision encoders (Tschannen et al., 2025; Radford et al., 2021; Oquab et al., 2023; He et al., 2022) produce the same representation of an image regardless of the query (Figure  1(a)). These representations capture broadly useful visual information but cannot explicitly prioritize the requested evidence (Ruthardt et al., 2026). More importantly, visual salience is not akin to query relevance: a prominent object may be irrelevant to the question, while a small detail may determine the answer. A useful visual representation should therefore be steerable: changing the query should change which visual information the representation emphasizes.

A separate limitation concerns how much representational capacity is allocated to that evidence. Visual tokenizers commonly produce a fixed-size sequence; ViT-based encoders (Oquab et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025) provides a fixed set of patch tokens, while the Q-Former uses a fixed number of latent tokens regardless of the image or the evidence required by the downstream task (Li et al., 2023). A large token budget increases downstream computation for every example (Yin et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2022; Li et al., 2026a), while a small budget may discard necessary details (Kim et al., 2026). These considerations expose two distinct axes of visual tokenization: which evidence to preserve and how much capacity to allocate (adaptivity), as shown in Fig. 1. These properties are increasingly relevant to embodied systems, where agents repeatedly interpret visual observations under changing goals, and efficient processing matters over long interaction horizons (Saxena et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2024). We seek a tokenizer that connects both axes, allocating capacity according to how well the current representation preserves query-relevant visual evidence.

Prior work addresses parts of this problem. Learned resamplers create compact latent representations, steerable encoders condition visual features on language (Ruthardt et al., 2026), and token-pruning methods remove redundant or query-irrelevant patches (Li et al., 2026a; Takezoe et al., 2026). Adaptive image tokenizers additionally vary their sequence length according to image complexity (Duggal et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2024). What remains less explored is an explicit mechanism that couples these choices: rather than prescribing a token count or predicting one directly, can a tokenizer continue allocating capacity until the evidence relevant to the current query has been represented with sufficient fidelity?

We introduce the Query-Adaptive Recurrent Tokenizer (QART), a visual tokenizer that converts dense encoder features into a variable-length set of query-conditioned visual tokens. Given frozen image features and a text query, a cross-modal relevance module first identifies the visual evidence relevant to the query. QART begins with a small set of tokens and recurrently refines them using this evidence and the query. After each round, a shared decoder reconstructs the relevant visual features, and reconstruction quality determines whether more tokens are added or computation halts. The resulting tokens form a compact representation whose content and capacity are both shaped by the query, and can be used by a downstream task head or language model.

We evaluate QART on prompt-conditioned retrieval (CORE (Ruthardt et al., 2026), GeneCIS (Vaze et al., 2023), PODS (Sundaram et al., 2025)), compositional matching (Winoground (Thrush et al., 2022)), Visual Question Answering (VQAv2 (Goyal et al., 2017)), and grounding (Visual7W pointing (Zhu et al., 2016). QART learns non-uniform allocations and compresses dense patch tokens by  25×\times. On CORE and GeneCIS, it improves over the query-agnostic SigLIP2 representation by 23.5% and 2.7% respectively. On Visual7W pointing, it outperforms the strongest token-reduction baseline DART Wen et al. (2025) by 22.1% under a matched protocol; on VQAv2, it retains 93.8% of dense accuracy while reducing tokens by 25×\times and outperforms a matched 32-token Q-Former, while improving end-to-end throughput by 1.53×\times. Together, these results highlight the significance of query-adaptive visual representations.

2 Related Work

2.1 Compact and Variable-Length Visual Tokenization

Vision encoders commonly represent an image as a dense grid of patch embeddings, motivating learned bottlenecks that summarize this grid with a smaller set of visual tokens (Bachmann et al., 2025). TokenLearner learns a compact set of content-adaptive tokens (Ryoo et al., 2021), while BLIP-2 uses a Querying Transformer (Q-Former) to map frozen image features into a fixed-size latent sequence for a downstream language model (Li et al., 2023). InstructBLIP further conditions the Q-Former on the input instruction, but retains a fixed latent budget (Dai et al., 2023). Matryoshka Query Transformer (MQT) supports multiple output lengths within one model by training nested prefixes of latent queries; however, the desired length is selected externally at inference time rather than inferred from the visual evidence required by each query (Hu et al., 2024).

Adaptive-length image tokenizers vary representation capacity with image content (Yan et al., 2024; Duggal et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). ALIT, the closest architectural precedent to our work, recurrently updates a latent sequence, adds tokens over successive rounds, and uses reconstruction as a learning signal for variable-length image representations (Duggal et al., 2025b). QART changes the unit of adaptation from the image alone to the image–query pair. Its text-conditioned relevance model determines which patch features must be preserved, and the recurrent tokenizer halts when those query-relevant features have been reconstructed sufficiently well. Consequently, the same image can produce different token contents and lengths under different queries.

2.2 Query-Conditioned and Steerable Visual Representations

Other work studies how language can steer visual representation (Mao et al., 2025). InstructBLIP extracts instruction-specific features through an instruction-aware Q-Former (Dai et al., 2023); FLAIR applies text-conditioned attention pooling to local image features for fine-grained retrieval (Xiao et al., 2025); and TIE conditions the image encoder on the text query (Thirukovalluru et al., 2025). SteerViT injects language into intermediate vision-transformer layers to produce dense visual features that can be directed toward a requested concept (Ruthardt et al., 2026). QMoP uses the query to route visual features among pooling, resampling, and pruning branches (Li et al., 2026b).

These methods establish that useful visual evidence depends on the language context; QART is therefore not the first query-conditioned visual representation. Its distinction lies in coupling query conditioning to recurrent capacity allocation. Rather than only changing which information is emphasized within a dense or prescribed-size representation, QART jointly determines what information to encode and how many latent tokens are required. The token count follows from an explicit representation-adequacy criterion instead of a fixed budget or a separately predicted length.

2.3 Visual Token Pruning and Merging

Visual-token reduction is also widely studied through pruning and merging (Chen et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Shang et al., 2025). ToMe reduces vision-transformer sequences by progressively merging similar tokens (Bolya et al., 2023). In vision-language systems, QG-VTC uses question–patch relevance to progressively compress visual tokens within the vision encoder (Li et al., 2025), while QuietPrune introduces query guidance early in the vision transformer so that pruning preserves prompt-relevant regions (Gao et al., 2026). ATP-LLaVA learns instance- and layer-dependent pruning ratios inside the language model (Ye et al., 2025); LearnPruner combines learned post-encoder reduction with query-guided pruning in intermediate language-model layers (Takezoe et al., 2026); and OccamToken derives image- and query-adaptive pruning thresholds without additional training (Li et al., 2026a).

These approaches primarily retain, merge, or discard existing tokens. QART instead constructs and recurrently expands a slot-based representation from frozen patch features until a query-conditioned reconstruction criterion is met, which supplies a shorter visual sequence to downstream models.

3 Method

QART converts dense encoder features into a variable-length sequence of query-conditioned visual tokens in three stages (Figure 2). A cross-modal relevance module selects query-relevant visual features (§3.1); a weight-shared recurrent Transformer then builds a slot-based representation from them, beginning with K0K_{0} query-initialized slots and adding Δ​K\Delta K new ones when reconstruction coverage of the selected features falls below a coverage criterion (§3.2–3.3). The trainable components are optimized jointly using query-weighted reconstruction and relevance-prediction objectives (§3.4).

3.1 Identifying Query-Relevant Evidence

Given an image I∈ℝH×W×3I\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3} and text query qq, QART represents the image–query pair as a variable-length set of steered visual tokens, or slots:

Gθ,ϕ,ψ​(I,q)=𝐒∈ℝK×D,K≤Kmax.G_{\theta,\phi,\psi}(I,q)=\mathbf{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D},\qquad K\leq K_{\max}. (1)

Frozen vision and text encoders produce visual features 𝐕=Ev​(I)∈ℝN×Dv\mathbf{V}=E_{\mathrm{v}}(I)\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D_{v}} and text tokens 𝐓=Et​(q)∈ℝL×Dt\mathbf{T}=E_{\mathrm{t}}(q)\in\mathbb{R}^{L\times D_{t}}, projected to a shared dimension DD. A cross-modal relevance module then predicts a relevance map 𝐏v\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{v}} which indicates how strongly each patch 𝐯i\mathbf{v}_{i} corresponds to the query:

𝐏v=[p1,p2,…,pN]T∈[0,1]N,pi=Hϕ​(𝐯i,𝐓),pi∈[0,1].\mathbf{P}_{\mathrm{v}}=[p_{1},p_{2},...,p_{N}]^{T}\in[0,1]^{N},\qquad p_{i}=H_{\phi}(\mathbf{v}_{i},\mathbf{T}),\qquad p_{i}\in[0,1]. (2)

This relevance map is used to identify the query-relevant support 𝒜={i∣pi>τ}\mathcal{A}=\{i\mid p_{i}>\tau\} and the corresponding features 𝐕𝒜={𝐯i}i∈𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}}=\{\mathbf{v}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{A}}. Having identified which evidence to preserve, the remaining problem is how to represent 𝐕𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}} compactly without prescribing a fixed token count.

3.2 Recurrent Query-Conditioned Representation

To answer the question, QART builds on progressive token allocation (Duggal et al., 2025b). Specifically, a pooled query representation 𝐪¯\bar{\mathbf{q}} seeds K0K_{0} initial slots through a learned projector, 𝐒(0)=finit​(𝐪¯)∈ℝK0×D\mathbf{S}^{(0)}=f_{\mathrm{init}}(\bar{\mathbf{q}})\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{0}\times D};these slots are then recurrently refined to gather evidence from 𝐕𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}}.

At each round rr, the slots 𝐒(r−1)\mathbf{S}^{(r-1)} interact with the selected visual features 𝐕𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}} and text through a shared Transformer FθF_{\theta}, followed by a cross-attention readout over 𝐕𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}}:

𝐒~(r)=Fθ​(𝐒(r−1),𝐕𝒜,𝐓),𝐒(r)=LN⁡(𝐒~(r)+MHA⁡(𝐒~(r),𝐕𝒜,𝐕𝒜)).\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}^{(r)}=F_{\theta}\!\left(\mathbf{S}^{(r-1)},\,\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}},\,\mathbf{T}\right),\qquad\mathbf{S}^{(r)}=\mathrm{LN}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}^{(r)}+\mathrm{MHA}\!\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{S}}^{(r)},\,\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}},\,\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}}\right)\right). (3)

When the current set of slots cannot represent 𝐕𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}} with sufficient fidelity , Δ​K\Delta K new slots are initialized from 𝐪¯\bar{\mathbf{q}} via finitf_{\mathrm{init}} and concatenated to the existing set before the next round, growing the representation from KrK_{r} to min⁡(Kr+Δ​K,Kmax)\min(K_{r}+\Delta K,\,K_{\max}).

3.3 Reconstruction-Guided Token Allocation

QART ties representation sufficiency to feature reconstruction. Specifically, after each round, a shared decoder DψD_{\psi} reconstructs the full visual feature grid from the current slots, producing 𝐕^(r)=Dψ​(𝐒(r))\widehat{\mathbf{V}}^{(r)}=D_{\psi}(\mathbf{S}^{(r)}). The per-patch reconstruction error is |𝐯^i(r)−𝐯i∥22/D|\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{(r)}-\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/D, evaluated only over 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The fraction of support patches whose error has dropped below a threshold δ\delta by round rr defines the reconstruction coverage:

c(r)=1|𝒜|∑i∈𝒜𝕀[|𝐯^i(r)−𝐯i∥22/D<δ].c^{(r)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{I}\!\left[\\ |\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{(r)}-\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/D<\delta\right]. (4)

If c(r)<ηgrowc^{(r)}<\eta_{\mathrm{grow}}, Δ​K\Delta K new slots are added before round r+1r{+}1:

Kr+1={min⁡(Kr+Δ​K,Kmax),c(r)<ηgrow,Kr,otherwise.K_{r+1}=\begin{cases}\min(K_{r}+\Delta K,\;K_{\max}),&c^{(r)}<\eta_{\mathrm{grow}},\\[2.84526pt] K_{r},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (5)

Recurrence halts once c(r)≥ηhaltc^{(r)}\geq\eta_{\mathrm{halt}}. Setting ηgrow<ηhalt\eta_{\mathrm{grow}}<\eta_{\mathrm{halt}} decouples the two decisions: slot addition can stop while the existing slots continue to refine. Because 𝒜\mathcal{A} depends on the query, the same image follows different allocation trajectories under different queries (App. C.3).

3.4 Learning Objective

Given soft relevance targets 𝐡∈[0,1]N\mathbf{h}\in[0,1]^{N} derived from segmentation or alignment annotations (App. A.1), we define per-patch importance weights ρi∗=hi/(∑jhj+ϵ)\rho_{i}^{*}=h_{i}/(\sum_{j}h_{j}+\epsilon) and the target support 𝒜∗={i∣hi>0}\mathcal{A}^{*}=\{i\mid h_{i}>0\}. The reconstruction loss weights each patch by its query relevance, averaged across all RR rounds:

ℒrec=1R∑r=1R∑i∈𝒜∗ρi∗|𝐯^i(r)−𝐯i∥22/D.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}^{*}}\rho_{i}^{*}\,|\widehat{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{(r)}-\mathbf{v}_{i}\|_{2}^{2}/D. (6)

The relevance module is trained with soft binary cross-entropy against 𝐡\mathbf{h}, denoted ℒrel\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}. The combined objective is

ℒ=λrec​ℒrec+λrel​ℒrel.\mathcal{L}=\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rec}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{rel}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rel}}. (7)

At inference, no relevance supervision is needed; the predicted relevance map and reconstruction coverage jointly determine the token count and number of recurrent rounds for each image–query pair.

4 Experiments

Our experiments probe the central properties of QART rather than performance on individual benchmarks alone. We ask whether query conditioning can steer a frozen visual representation toward the requested content, whether the resulting compact representation preserves downstream reasoning, whether its behavior genuinely depends on the query, whether it retains information beyond what the query explicitly specifies, and whether its compactness translates into practical inference gains.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Unless stated otherwise, QART uses frozen SigLIP2 vision and text encoders and produces at most 32 visual tokens from 729 patch features. A single pretrained QART checkpoint is used across the representation benchmarks without task-specific finetuning. For VQA, QART replaces the visual tokens of LLaVA-1.5-7B while both QART and the language model remain frozen; only a lightweight visual projector is trained. Full architecture, training, and evaluation details are provided in the appendix A. We additionally evaluate backbone generalization by using DINOv2 in App. B.

4.2 Does QART Redirect a Pretrained Visual Representation?

We first ask whether QART changes what a frozen visual representation encodes. If query conditioning is effective, the resulting representation should emphasize the visual evidence requested by the query rather than simply inherit the dominant semantics of the pretrained backbone.

Controlled evaluation on CORE.

CORE Ruthardt et al. (2026) 11 1 We follow SteerViT’s protocol for CORE. directly tests this behavior by requiring retrieval according to a queried object that may occupy only a small part of the image. QART reaches 92.0%92.0\% P@1, compared with 68.5%68.5\% for the native SigLIP2 global representation (Fig. 3a). Because both representations originate from the same frozen vision encoder, this improvement isolates the effect of query-conditioned representation construction. QART therefore does more than compress the underlying patch features; it changes which visual evidence dominates the representation. QART also outperforms open-vocabulary localization methods like Grounding-DINO (Liu et al., 2024) and SteerViT (Ruthardt et al., 2026) showcasing the benefit of query-relevant adaptive representations.

Does the same behavior transfer to natural images?

We next test whether this steering behavior transfers beyond the controlled CORE setting. On GeneCIS Focus Object, QART uses the same pretrained checkpoint without GeneCIS-specific tuning. It improves over native SigLIP2 representations by 2.72.7, 5.05.0, and 7.17.1% at R@1, R@2, and R@3, respectively (Fig. 3b).

The gain increases with retrieval depth, suggesting that query conditioning consistently promotes condition-compatible images throughout the ranked list rather than affecting only the top prediction. QART also improves over simple Image + Text composition at every rank and approaches Combiner, despite Combiner being designed specifically for composed image-text retrieval.

4.3 Can QART Preserve Reasoning and Grounding Under Extreme Visual Compression?

Steering a representation is useful only if the resulting compact tokens retain the information required downstream. We test this in two complementary settings. VQAv2 evaluates general visual reasoning, while Visual7W places greater emphasis on grounding and localized visual evidence.

General reasoning on VQAv2.

Replacing the dense visual tokens of LLaVA-1.5-7B+SigLIP2 with QART tokens, QART reaches 76.37% acc., retaining 93.8% of dense accuracy (81.4%) with 24.8× fewer tokens, and outperforms a matched 32-token Q-Former by 1.7%. Pruning baselines use a different base model, so we compare relative accuracies (Tab. 1a); strong pruners retain slightly more performance here, as VQAv2’s general questions limit the benefit of query-directed representation.

Grounded reasoning on Visual7W.

We next test whether this compact representation preserves the spatially localized evidence required for grounding in Tab. 1b. We specifically focus on the pointing task as it requires selecting the box that answers a question, so evidence at specific locations must be preserved. Under a matched pipeline (App. A.3), QART reaches 81.96% with 29 tokens, retaining 92.6% of dense model’s accuracy and outperforming the strongest baseline, DART, by 22.1%. This larger gap indicates that aggressive compression is more demanding when predictions depend on localized visual evidence. Nevertheless, QART retains substantially more grounding information than existing low-token pruning methods. This suggests that query-conditioned token construction preserves the spatial evidence needed to associate the query with relevant image regions.

Does recurrence refine the representation?

To isolate recurrent refinement from token growth, we evaluate the same QART checkpoint while fixing the representation to two slots throughout recurrence, such that no additional slots are added. VQAv2 accuracy increases from 46.27%46.27\% after one round to 50.93%50.93\% after three rounds and remains around that number thereafter (Fig. 4a). Since both the query-relevant support and token count remain fixed, this improvement shows that recurrent updates can refine the representation independently of increasing its capacity. Additional qualitative results are provided in App. C.2.

4.4 Does the Conditioning Query Actually Control the Representation?

We use Winoground (Thrush et al., 2022) to test whether QART responds to the compositional meaning of the conditioning query. The benchmark pairs two images with two captions that contain the same words but differ in composition, and evaluates whether the model matches each caption to the correct image. We emphasize Image accuracy, where both candidate images are conditioned on the same caption, and Group accuracy, which additionally requires the Text judgment to be correct.

QART reaches 24.75%24.75\% Image and 19.25%19.25\% Group accuracy, compared with 19.75%19.75\% and 17.00%17.00\% for native SigLIP2. It also has 36.25% text accuracy. Further, it outperforms stronger models like FLAVA (Singh et al., 2022) and Vin-VL (Hu et al., 2022) comfortably. More importantly, replacing the sample-specific query with a fixed query reduces Image accuracy to 15.25%15.25\% and Group accuracy to 12.00%12.00\% (Fig. 3c).

This controlled intervention isolates the effect of conditioning from the tokenizer itself, showing that QART changes its visual representation according to the compositional meaning of the query rather than only the words it contains. Sec. 4.7. further probes the impact of query conditioning in representation steering and adaptive token allocation.

4.5 Does Query Conditioning Preserve Information Beyond the Prompt?

Query-conditioned compression introduces a complementary risk. A representation may become highly focused on the prompt while discarding visual detail that the prompt does not explicitly mention. We test this on PODS, where QART receives only a coarse supercategory prompt, such as “mug” or “shoe”, but must distinguish a particular object from visually similar instances of the same category.

QART reaches 36.3%36.3\% PR-AUC and 61.3%61.3\% NDCG, improving PR-AUC by 8.48.4% over SteerViT under the same supercategory prompting setting and by 6.76.7% over unconditioned DINOv2 (Fig. 3d).

The query itself cannot identify the correct instance. QART must therefore use it to determine which region or semantic content is relevant while still preserving visual cues that are more specific than the language supervision. The improvement on PODS shows that steering does not collapse the representation to only what is explicitly stated in the prompt. Instead, the query determines where representational capacity is focused while fine-grained visual information within that region is retained.

4.6 Does Compactness Translate into Real Inference Gains?

A shorter visual sequence is useful only if the reduction offsets the cost of constructing it. We therefore measure end-to-end VLM inference as batch size increases.

At batch size one, QART’s recurrent tokenization introduces more overhead than is recovered by the shorter language-model sequence, resulting in a 0.87×0.87\times end-to-end speed ratio. The balance changes as batch size increases and processing the visual sequence inside the language model becomes more expensive. At batch size four, QART reaches 1.14×1.14\times end-to-end and 1.84×1.84\times prefill speed-up. At batch size eight, these gains increase to 1.53×1.53\times and 2.54×2.54\times, respectively, with throughput increasing from 21.021.0 to 32.232.2 samples/s (Fig. 4).

The different scaling of tokenization and language-model processing explains this trend. QART incurs a largely fixed cost to construct its representation, while reducing the sequence subsequently processed by the 7B language model. Its advantage therefore becomes larger when downstream sequence processing dominates the computation.

4.7 What Does Query Conditioning Control?

Query conditioning enters QART in two places. It determines the visual support available during recurrent refinement, and it defines the evidence used by the reconstruction coverage c(r)c^{(r)} to control slot growth and halting. We ablate these two roles on CORE, and illustrate the results in Tab. 2.

Making the budget decisions query-agnostic has almost no effect on retrieval accuracy, but removes the computational adaptivity of QART. The model reaches 92.08%92.08\% P@1, yet activates all 3232 slots and runs all six rounds. Using query-relevant evidence for growth and halting preserves essentially the same accuracy while reducing the average budget to 17.2517.25 slots and 4.254.25 rounds. This corresponds to roughly 46%46\% fewer active tokens and 29%29\% fewer recurrent rounds.

The query-relevant support itself plays a different role. When the relevance threshold τ\tau is set to zero, all patches participate rather than focusing recurrence on the queried evidence. When there is no query-conditioning for the visual support, P@1 drops to 79.7%79.7\%, still outperforming the SigLIP2 number. Thus, query conditioning of the visual support is important for steering the representation, whereas query conditioning of the reconstruction coverage enables efficient allocation of capacity.

5 Conclusion

We introduced QART, a recurrent visual tokenizer that combines query steerability with budget adaptivity. QART steers its representation toward query-relevant evidence and allocates additional visual tokens only when that evidence is not yet represented with sufficient fidelity. Across retrieval, grounding, compositional matching, and visual question answering, QART produces compact representations with substantially fewer tokens while preserving strong downstream performance. Its gains are strongest when predictions depend on localized visual evidence, while on general VQA it remains competitive with existing token-reduction methods. Overall, these results show that visual representations need not be fixed in either content or capacity, and can instead be shaped by what each query requires.

Ethics Statement

This work uses publicly available datasets and pretrained models and does not involve new human-subject data collection. As with other vision and vision–language systems, QART may inherit biases and limitations from its training data and pretrained encoders. Any downstream deployment should therefore consider the provenance and biases of the underlying data and models, as well as the requirements of the target application.

Reproducibility Statement

To the best of my knowledge, all the necessary details needed to reproduce the results have been provided in the main paper and appendix. However, the code cannot be released as this projected was conducted with an industrial partner which limits us. However, if absolutely necessary, we can try to release the necessary supplementary materials.

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 Datasets

Tokenizer pretraining data.

We pretrain QART on a mixture of referring-expression, scene-understanding, and region-description datasets comprising RefCOCO Yu et al. (2016), RefCOCO+ Yu et al. (2016), RefCOCOg Yu et al. (2016), gRefCOCO Liu et al. (2023a), Mapillary Vistas Neuhold et al. (2017), and Visual Genome (VG) Krishna et al. (2017). The complete mixture contains 2,078,3672{,}078{,}367 image–text annotation records; this number counts annotations rather than unique images. Table 3 summarizes the sampling distribution. Training examples are sampled with replacement according to the specified mixture weights.

Query-relevance supervision.

During tokenizer pretraining, we use dense query-region targets to supervise the relevance predictor, following Ruthardt et al. (Ruthardt et al., 2026). For the COCO-family referring-expression datasets (Yu et al., 2016), relevance targets are derived from segmentation annotations. For Mapillary Vistas (Neuhold et al., 2017) and Visual Genome (Krishna et al., 2017), we use cached dense query-region alignment maps. The resulting heatmaps are retained as soft targets in [0,1][0,1] rather than being converted to binary bounding boxes. These targets provide training supervision for the relevance predictor and the query-weighted reconstruction objective, but are not used to define the visual support or the recurrent growth and halting decisions. The recurrent tokenizer instead operates on the support predicted by the relevance module, 𝒜={i∣pi>τ}\mathcal{A}=\{i\mid p_{i}>\tau\}, both during training and inference.

Vision–language alignment data.

For integration with LLaVA-1.5-7B Liu et al. (2023b), we train the visual projector in two stages. The first stage performs one epoch of Visual Genome-based alignment using native-image VG region descriptions. The region phrase conditions QART, while the language model receives a generic region-description instruction and predicts the corresponding phrase.

The second stage trains the projector for one epoch on the full LLaVA-Instruct-665K mixture Liu et al. (2023b). QART and the language model remain frozen throughout both stages, and only the visual projector is optimized.

A.2 Setup

Backbone and input representations.

Our main configuration uses the frozen vision and text encoders from google/siglip2-so400m-patch14-384. Images are processed at 384×384384\times 384 resolution. The visual encoder produces a 27×2727\times 27 grid of N=729N=729 patch features, each with dimension 11521152. We precompute and cache these frozen visual features in FP16.

A bias-free linear layer projects the visual features to the tokenizer dimension D=768D=768.

The frozen text encoder provides token-level query representations, which are projected to the same 768768-dimensional space when necessary. Padding tokens are masked, and a masked mean of the query features is used to initialize the slot bank. Tokenizer pretraining uses a maximum text length of 32 tokens.

The reconstruction target is the projected visual feature map used by the tokenizer. Specifically, the frozen backbone features are first projected to the tokenizer dimension, and the decoder reconstructs these projected visual features rather than RGB pixels.

Relevance predictor.

The relevance predictor consists of five visual-to-text cross-attention layers with eight attention heads. Visual patches act as queries and text tokens as keys and values. Each layer uses pre-layer normalization (Nguyen and Salazar, 2019) and a residual connection without an intermediate feed-forward block. A final linear projection followed by a sigmoid predicts one relevance score pi∈[0,1]p_{i}\in[0,1] for each visual patch.

Queries and keys are normalized independently within each attention head after their learned projections. At inference, the query-relevant visual support is defined as

𝒜={i∣pi>τ}.\mathcal{A}=\{i\mid p_{i}>\tau\}. (8)

The relevance set is computed once before recurrence and remains fixed across recurrent rounds. For tasks in which a visual target is guaranteed to exist, an empty selection falls back to the 100 patches with the highest relevance scores.

Recurrent tokenizer.

QART maintains at most Kmax=32K_{\max}=32 active latent slots. A masked mean of the query-token representations produces a pooled query representation 𝐪¯\bar{\mathbf{q}}. At initialization, a learned slot projector finitf_{\mathrm{init}} maps 𝐪¯\bar{\mathbf{q}} to K0=2K_{0}=2 query-conditioned slots,

𝐒(0)=finit​(𝐪¯)∈ℝK0×D.\mathbf{S}^{(0)}=f_{\mathrm{init}}(\bar{\mathbf{q}})\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{0}\times D}. (9)

The projector produces distinct slot embeddings from the shared query representation, followed by per-slot layer normalization.

Each recurrent round uses a three-layer pre-normalized Transformer with eight attention heads and a feed-forward width of 3072. The complete three-layer Transformer is shared across recurrent rounds, while the three layers within the block use distinct parameters. Learned modality embeddings distinguish slot, visual, and text tokens, and a learned round embedding is added to the active slots.

At round rr, the shared Transformer jointly processes the current slots 𝐒(r−1)\mathbf{S}^{(r-1)}, the selected query-relevant visual features 𝐕𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}}, and the text features 𝐓\mathbf{T}:

𝐒~(r)=Fθ​(𝐒(r−1),𝐕𝒜,𝐓).\tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{(r)}=F_{\theta}\left(\mathbf{S}^{(r-1)},\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}},\mathbf{T}\right). (10)

A subsequent slot-to-patch cross-attention readout allows the resulting slots to gather additional information from the selected visual evidence:

𝐒(r)=LN⁡(𝐒~(r)+MHA⁡(𝐒~(r),𝐕𝒜,𝐕𝒜)).\mathbf{S}^{(r)}=\mathrm{LN}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{(r)}+\mathrm{MHA}\left(\tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{(r)},\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}},\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}}\right)\right). (11)

Only the slot states 𝐒(r)\mathbf{S}^{(r)} are propagated recurrently. The selected visual features 𝐕𝒜\mathbf{V}_{\mathcal{A}} and text features 𝐓\mathbf{T} remain fixed and are supplied again at every round.

The joint self-attention uses per-head QK normalization. We additionally use shared learned residual-scaling parameters

𝐔=α​𝐗+β​SA​(LN⁡(𝐗)),\mathbf{U}=\alpha\mathbf{X}+\beta\,\mathrm{SA}\!\left(\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{X})\right), (12)
𝐗′=α​𝐔+β​FFN​(LN⁡(𝐔)),\mathbf{X}^{\prime}=\alpha\mathbf{U}+\beta\,\mathrm{FFN}\!\left(\mathrm{LN}(\mathbf{U})\right), (13)

initialized to α=0.75\alpha=0.75 and β=0.25\beta=0.25.

When the current slot set does not represent the selected visual evidence with sufficient fidelity, Δ​K=6\Delta K=6 additional slots are initialized from 𝐪¯\bar{\mathbf{q}} using finitf_{\mathrm{init}} and concatenated with the existing slots before the next recurrent round. The active slot count therefore follows

Kr+1={min⁡(Kr+Δ​K,Kmax),c(r)<ηgrow,Kr,otherwise.K_{r+1}=\begin{cases}\min(K_{r}+\Delta K,K_{\max}),&c^{(r)}<\eta_{\mathrm{grow}},\\ K_{r},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (14)

Reconstruction and adaptive computation.

A shared decoder reconstructs the dense visual feature grid from the active slots after each recurrent round. The decoder uses NN learned positional queries and four pre-normalized cross-attention/FFN blocks, with the active slots supplying keys and values. Each block uses eight attention heads and a feed-forward width of 4​D4D. A final layer normalization and linear projection produce the reconstructed visual features 𝐕^(r)∈ℝN×D\hat{\mathbf{V}}^{(r)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}.

For visual feature 𝐯i∈ℝD\mathbf{v}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} and its reconstruction 𝐯^i(r)\hat{\mathbf{v}}^{(r)}_{i} at round rr, we compute the normalized squared reconstruction error as

1D​‖𝐯^i(r)−𝐯i‖22.\frac{1}{D}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{(r)}-\mathbf{v}_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (15)

Representation completion at round rr is measured over the selected query-relevant support,

c(r)=1|𝒜|∑i∈𝒜𝕀[1D‖𝐯^i(r)−𝐯i‖22<δ].c^{(r)}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{A}}\mathbb{I}\left[\frac{1}{D}\left\|\hat{\mathbf{v}}_{i}^{(r)}-\mathbf{v}_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}<\delta\right]. (16)

We use δ=0.30\delta=0.30, ηgrow=0.85\eta_{\mathrm{grow}}=0.85, and ηhalt=0.95\eta_{\mathrm{halt}}=0.95. If c(r)<ηgrowc^{(r)}<\eta_{\mathrm{grow}}, up to six additional slots are activated, subject to the 3232-slot limit. The resulting maximum-capacity sequence is 2,8,14,20,26,322,8,14,20,26,32. Inference may halt after a minimum of two recurrent rounds once c(r)≥ηhaltc^{(r)}\geq\eta_{\mathrm{halt}}, and otherwise continues for at most six rounds. During tokenizer pretraining, all six rounds are executed while slot growth remains adaptive.

Tokenizer optimization.

We optimize the trainable QART components using AdamW with learning rate 10−410^{-4}, (β1,β2)=(0.9,0.999)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2})=(0.9,0.999), and weight decay 0.010.01. The learning rate increases linearly for 4,000 optimizer steps and then follows a cosine schedule over 25 epochs. Training uses a global batch size of 256, BF16 mixed precision, and global-norm gradient clipping at 0.50.5.

The training objective combines query-weighted feature reconstruction and relevance prediction as described in Sec. 3.4. We use λrec=1\lambda_{\mathrm{rec}}=1 and λrel=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{rel}}=0.5. The implementation additionally includes a slot-count term with weight 0.010.01. Because slot allocation is discrete, this term does not propagate gradients through the allocation decisions.

Vision–language projector.

For LLaVA-1.5-7B, the active QART slots are mapped to the language-model embedding dimension using a two-layer projector

768→4096→4096,768\rightarrow 4096\rightarrow 4096, (17)

with input layer normalization, GELU activation, and output layer normalization.

Both projector-training stages use AdamW with learning rate 2×10−42\times 10^{-4}, zero weight decay, a 500-step linear warmup followed by cosine decay, and gradient-norm clipping at 1.01.0. The global batch size is 32. The first Visual Genome alignment stage is run for one epoch, followed by one epoch on LLaVA-Instruct-665K. Only the projector parameters are updated in both stages.

A.3 Evaluation Protocols

Shared representation evaluation.

CORE, GeneCIS, PODS, and Winoground use the frozen pretrained QART tokenizer without benchmark-specific fitting. For retrieval-style evaluations, we mean-pool the active slots, compute the representation in FP32, apply ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization, and use cosine similarity.

Unless stated otherwise, transfer experiments use the same SigLIP2 QART checkpoint and the relevance threshold τ=0.25\tau=0.25. GeneCIS, PODS, and Winoground execute each image–query pair independently so that recurrent halting is determined per example.

CORE.

We evaluate on the JonaRuthardt/CORE test split using the provided scene-specific galleries and object prompts. For each target object, all images in its gallery are encoded under the same query. Each positive image is used as a retrieval query, while itself and variants of the same source image are excluded from the gallery. We report precision at rank one (P@1) over the eligible retrieval queries.

GeneCIS.

We evaluate the GeneCIS Vaze et al. (2023) Focus Object split. For every query, the reference image and its 15 candidate images are encoded using the same object condition. Candidate membership from the benchmark is preserved without introducing additional negatives. Candidates are ranked using cosine similarity between normalized mean-slot representations, and we report R@1, R@2, and R@3.

VQAv2.

For VQAv2 Goyal et al. (2017), we use the QART–LLaVA-1.5-7B model obtained after the two-stage projector training described above. QART and the 7B language model remain frozen, and the relevance threshold is set to τ=0.05\tau=0.05. Only active QART slots are projected into the language-model embedding space and inserted before the textual question.

Answers are generated autoregressively using greedy decoding. We use at most 16 generated tokens and evaluate predictions using the standard VQAv2 evaluation protocol.

For VQAv2, we reproduce LLaVA+SigLIP2 where the visual representations are replaced with siglip tokens, and Q-Former Li et al. (2023) by following the same protocol as QART. The other numbers are reported from their corresponding papers.

Visual7W.

For Visual7W, we evaluate it on the pointing task. For the pointing task, the 4 candidate bounding boxes are given in [x1, y1, x2, y2] format. Also, the 4 candidates are given as A, B, C and D to the LLM, and the answer is always one of the 4 alphabets. Evaluation is normal accuracy checking for a perfect match.

We reproduce all compared methods under a common evaluation pipeline. We use the LLaVA+SigLIP2 configuration as the base model for all the pruning baselines which is finetuned with the same protocol as qart, which is one epoch of vg-alignment and 6 epochs of Visual7W projector finetuning. And for all learnable baselines, we additionally finetune for 4 epochs on Visual7W data to adapt to the compressed representations.

Winoground.

We evaluate all 400 official Winoground Thrush et al. (2022) examples and score all four image–caption pairings. For an image IiI_{i} conditioned on caption cjc_{j}, QART reconstructs the visual feature grid from its active slots. We then apply the frozen SigLIP2 attention pooler and compute cosine similarity with the native SigLIP2 text representation,

Si​j=cos⁡(Hv​(V^​(Ii,cj)),Ht​(cj)).S_{ij}=\cos\left(H_{v}\bigl(\hat{V}(I_{i},c_{j})\bigr),H_{t}(c_{j})\right). (18)

We compute the official Text, Image, and Group accuracies from the resulting 2×22\times 2 similarity matrix. For the fixed-query control, the same generic text query is used to condition QART for every image while the official Winoground scoring protocol remains unchanged.

PODS.

We follow the PODS Sundaram et al. (2025) evaluation protocol over 100 target objects, 300 reference images, and 10,888 test images. For the main experiment, the dataset’s coarse supercategory label is used as the conditioning query for all reference and test images associated with a target object.

For classification, each test image is scored by its maximum cosine similarity to the three positive reference representations. We compute average precision independently for each target object and report the macro average. For retrieval, each positive test image ranks all 300 references, with the three references belonging to the same target object treated as relevant. We compute binary NDCG over the complete ranking and average first within each target object and then across objects.

Appendix B Evaluating Backbone generalization with DINOv2

B.1 Data and Setup

We additionally train QART using frozen DINOv2-B/14 visual features and a frozen RoBERTa-large text encoder. Images are resized to 378×378378\times 378, producing a 27×2727\times 27 grid of 729729 patch features with dimension 768768 after removing the CLS token. RoBERTa-large provides the query features, which are projected to the same 768768-dimensional tokenizer space.

The remaining QART architecture is unchanged from the SigLIP2 configuration. We use the same relevance predictor, recurrent tokenizer, reconstruction decoder, slot-allocation policy, training objective, data mixture, optimizer, and training schedule described in Sec. A. The model uses two initial slots, a maximum of 3232 slots, and at most six recurrent rounds.

The DINOv2 configuration differs from the main SigLIP2 model in an important respect. SigLIP2 jointly pretrains its visual and textual representations, whereas DINOv2 and RoBERTa are independently pretrained and do not share a cross-modal embedding space. Consequently, the DINOv2–RoBERTa configuration provides a weaker initialization for query-conditioned visual representation learning despite using the same QART architecture.

VQAv2 setup.

For VQAv2 Goyal et al. (2017), we follow the same protocol as followed for the SigLIP2 QART variant.

B.2 Results

CORE.

We evaluate DINOv2 QART using the same CORE protocol as the SigLIP2 model. The relevance threshold is applied to the predicted patch-relevance scores, and image representations are obtained by mean pooling the active slots, followed by ℓ2\ell_{2} normalization and cosine similarity.

At τ=0.25\tau=0.25, DINOv2 QART reaches 90.33%90.33\% P@1 with 23.3423.34 active slots on average. Its best recorded operating point reaches 90.59%90.59\% P@1 at τ=0.20\tau=0.20. For comparison, the SigLIP2 QART configuration reaches 92.01%92.01\% P@1 at τ=0.25\tau=0.25.

The relatively small gap on CORE indicates that the adaptive tokenization mechanism transfers effectively to DINOv2 features, despite the absence of a jointly pretrained vision–language representation.

VQAv2.

We evaluate the DINOv2 variant using the same LLaVA-1.5-7B integration and projector-training protocol as the SigLIP2 QART model. The results are shown in Tab. 4.

Under the matched training protocol, the DINOv2 variant reaches 72.93%72.93\% overall accuracy compared with 76.37%76.37\% for SigLIP2 QART. The largest difference appears on number questions, while the gap is smaller for yes/no questions. DINOv2 also uses slightly more active slots on average.

Although the DINOv2 variant trails SigLIP2, its VQAv2 performance remains competitive with prior visual-token pruning and reduction methods operating at similarly aggressive token budgets, as reported in the main paper. This indicates that the QART formulation remains effective even when the visual and textual encoders are not jointly pretrained.

We attribute the remaining gap primarily to the weaker cross-modal initialization of the independently pretrained DINOv2 and RoBERTa encoders, which lack the native vision–language alignment available in SigLIP2.

B.3 Discussion

The DINOv2 results show that QART is not tied to a particular visual backbone. The variant remains close to SigLIP2 on CORE and retains competitive VQAv2 performance at a compact visual-token budget, despite using independently pretrained vision and text encoders.

The stronger SigLIP2 results are consistent with the benefit of native cross-modal alignment. SigLIP2 jointly learns visual and textual representations, whereas DINOv2 and RoBERTa are pretrained independently and therefore provide a weaker starting point for query-conditioned representation learning. We therefore view the DINOv2 experiments as evidence that QART generalizes across backbone families, while also highlighting the importance of aligned vision–language features for its strongest performance.

Appendix C Additional Results and Analyses for QART

C.1 Threshold Sensitivity and Adaptive Budgeting

The relevance threshold τ\tau controls the spatial support selected for recurrent tokenization. Changing this threshold therefore affects both which image regions are represented and the amount of representational capacity subsequently allocated by QART. We analyze this interaction on CORE, GeneCIS, and Winoground using the same SigLIP2 QART model.

Table 5 reports the primary metric for each task together with the resulting mean active-slot count when available. For CORE, we report P@1; for GeneCIS, R@1; and for Winoground, Group accuracy.

The optimal operating point differs across tasks. CORE performs best at τ=0.25\tau=0.25, whereas GeneCIS reaches its highest R@1 at τ=0.20\tau=0.20. Winoground also favors an intermediate threshold rather than either extreme.

More importantly, increasing the selected visual support and the resulting token budget does not guarantee improved performance. On GeneCIS, lowering the threshold from 0.200.20 to 0.050.05 increases the mean slot count from 25.3825.38 to 30.0430.04, yet R@1 decreases from 15.10%15.10\% to 12.81%12.81\%. A similar pattern appears on Winoground, where τ=0.10\tau=0.10 uses 31.0731.07 slots on average but obtains lower Group accuracy than τ=0.25\tau=0.25, which uses only 27.4927.49 slots.

These results highlight that QART’s budget should not be interpreted as a simple “more tokens is better” trade-off. The relevance threshold jointly controls the spatial extent and composition of the selected evidence, while the recurrent tokenizer allocates capacity to represent that evidence. Different tasks therefore favor different combinations of visual coverage and token budget.

Broader coverage generally increases the available token budget, but additional tokens do not monotonically improve downstream performance. The task-dependent optima suggest that a single fixed visual budget or uniformly holistic representation is unlikely to be optimal across different visual reasoning settings.

C.2 Does Recurrence Refine the Representation?

QART does not construct its representation in a single step. The active slots are repeatedly refined using the same query and visual evidence, allowing their spatial support to change across recurrent rounds. Figure 5 shows representative examples of this behavior.

The progression is particularly clear when the initial representation attends to a nearby distractor or only coarsely identifies the relevant region. For the query “person in foreground with backpack,” the early support is spread over nearby foreground content before progressively concentrating on the queried person and backpack. A similar shift occurs for “guy in plaid,” where the support moves toward the queried individual over successive rounds. For “number 13,” the representation initially responds to nearby players before becoming localized around the jersey number of the target player.

These examples suggest that recurrence provides more than additional representational capacity. Later rounds can revise where the active slots attend, progressively moving their support toward evidence that is better aligned with the query. This is useful when the relevant region is visually ambiguous or surrounded by similar content, where a single tokenization step may commit too early to an incorrect or overly broad region.

C.3 Is QART query-steerable and budget-adaptive?

Figure 6 qualitatively illustrates how the conditioning query changes the visual representation. For the same input image, QART shifts its support from the left pizza to the right pizza when the query changes. Importantly, the representation does not only move spatially: the active token budget also changes from K=8K=8 to K=20K=20. This provides a direct example of query steerability and budget adaptivity within the same image.

The allocated capacity also varies substantially across different image–query pairs. Figure 7 shows representative examples spanning K=2K=2 to the full K=32K=32 slot budget. Localized targets such as “zebra on far right” and “top right bowl” require only a small representation, whereas other queries receive substantially more capacity. Queries involving broader or spatially distributed evidence can activate most or all of the available slots.

The token count is not determined by the number of queried objects alone. Instead, it reflects the visual evidence that QART needs to preserve for a particular image–query pair, including its spatial extent, appearance, and surrounding context. Together, Figs. 6 and 7 show that QART adapts both the content and the capacity of its representation rather than applying a fixed visual budget to every query.

C.4 Limitations

While QART is evaluated across retrieval, compositional matching, visual question answering, and grounding, our experiments focus on single-image settings. Extending query-adaptive token allocation to video, multi-turn interaction, and temporally evolving visual observations remains an interesting direction for future work.

The current formulation also uses a small number of thresholds to control relevance selection, slot growth, and halting. As shown in our sensitivity analysis, the preferred operating point can vary across tasks. Exploring fully learned or calibration-free allocation criteria could further simplify deployment across heterogeneous downstream settings.

Finally, QART uses dense query-region supervision during tokenizer pretraining to train the relevance predictor and reconstruction objective. This supervision is not required at inference, but future work could investigate weaker or self-supervised relevance signals to reduce the annotation requirements of tokenizer pretraining.
